title: Warsh says rise of AI will prove ‘very bumpy,’ trigger demand shock
source_used: CFO Dive, read on Yahoo Finance
key_facts: Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh spoke on Friday at the International Monetary Fund's annual meeting in Bangkok.
He called the rise of AI probably the most consequential change to the US and global economy in his lifetime, and said the path there is likely to be very bumpy.
He said AI is hitting the demand side of the economy before the supply side, and predicted a supply shock in the medium term and a huge benefit to the global economy.
Large technology companies (hyperscalers) are rushing to secure electricity, cooling, servers and chips, which has jarred the US economy for several months.
Since mid-September, hyperscaler borrowing helped push the yield on the 10-year Treasury note beyond 5%, raising borrowing costs for consumers and businesses.

IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva warned in a blog that a market correction could cascade through the highly leveraged and circular AI ecosystem; Gartner said more than $3.5 trillion of AI infrastructure spending may be exposed to impairment by the end of 2030.
quote_evidence: "The advent of this new technology is probably the most consequential change to the U.S. and the global economy in my lifetime," Warsh said at the annual meeting of the International Monetary Fund in Bangkok.

AI is "obviously hitting the demand side of the economy before it's going to hit the supply side of the economy," he said, predicting a supply shock in the medium term and "a huge benefit to the global economy, to the U.S. economy."
Since mid-September borrowing by the hyperscalers helped push up the yield on the benchmark 10-year treasury note beyond 5%, increasing the cost of borrowing for consumers and businesses.
why_it_matters_hint: The head of the US central bank calls AI a major economic shock, and heavy AI borrowing has helped push the 10-year yield above 5%, which raises costs for borrowers.
notes: Read on Yahoo Finance, which carries CFO Dive's text. Warsh's quotes are in the article; the borrowing and yield figures are the article's own statements, not Warsh's.
